Inspection spacing and measurement noise
In this realization, the three accepted violating lots are explained by measurement noise rather than by the sampling interval (Table S15). Windows of 15 m lie entirely within a lot, 850 at the 0.1-m grid and 170 at the 0.5-m spacing. The noiseless violating fractions of the three lots were 5.1–6.2% at 0.1 m and 5.3–5.9% at 0.5 m, both above the 5% limit, whereas the noisy offsets gave 2.9–3.5%; small exceedances can be cancelled by 1-mm errors. The miss count is, however, not a stable property of the procedure (Table S17): with another realization of the 1-mm noise, 7 of the 91 violating lots were accepted; with a noiseless survey at 0.5 m, 12 were accepted, because the 0.5-m spacing misses short exceedances that define a violation at 0.1 m; and survey errors of 2 and 3 mm reduced the misses to 1 and 0 but rejected 832 and 2,554 conforming lots. Measurement noise inflates window ranges and thus trades missed violations for false rejections, so a verification rule must define the alignment requirement at the spacing and precision of the inspection it uses. Over the 3,955 position-accepted lots, coarsening from 0.1 to 0.5 m changed the classification of 13 lots, whereas the measurement noise changed 124 (121 from conforming to violating, which explains most of the 107 conforming lots rejected by the survey). The screen sent 3,337 of the 3,955 position-accepted lots to the survey and reduced the number of simulated survey offsets by only 16% compared with surveying every lot; this is a count of simulated measurements, not a measured saving of time or cost. That no violating lot remained unsurveyed at  mm is an observation in this simulation, not a general guarantee for lots that are accepted without a survey.

Additional detailed results and validation design
The following passages retain details condensed in the final manuscript. Figure and table numbers in these passages refer to the final main manuscript and its supplements.
The research questions concern computable and traceable acceptance (RQ1), clause-dependent error budgets and mission effects (RQ2), and risk-calibrated fusion of logs and checks with a separate alignment decision (RQ3).
The central contribution is a mission-aware, traceable procedure for statistical position acceptance of robot-placed lines that fuses the dense log with sparse independent checks. It rests on a mission-dependent covariance used for kriging, analytical error budgets for position and window-range clauses, plans calibrated with a distribution-free bound and evaluated on independent lots, and a knowledge model constrained by the Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) and aligned with the PROV-O, SOSA, and QUDT ontologies. Ordinary kriging, SHACL, and distribution-free calibration are established methods; the contribution lies in their integration and in the mission covariance, whose value is tested by a paired ablation. Fig. 1 summarizes the framework.
On 196,000 interior lots (20 cells of 100 runs of 10 km; Table S21 shows the cell  mm, zero bias; Table S14 maps all samples), five-point attribute checks, which resemble current spot checks, accepted 44.7% of nonconforming lots at  mm. Compared at a matched consumer risk of 10%, kriging with three new checks per lot had a producer risk indistinguishable from that of a 20-point variables survey (0.138 against 0.135) and 0.097 with five checks; standard errors from a bootstrap over whole runs were 0.008–0.009 (Table S21). With thresholds calibrated on 4,000 independent lots and tested on 4,000 others in five scenarios, the realized consumer risks were 3.3–6.7% (Table 2, Fig. 5). Five new checks per lot with the log had a lower producer risk than the 20-point survey in four scenarios, for example 16.2% against 24.8% on a straight route and 21.1% against 36.4% in the exact closed loop with a 0.5-m lever. On the 15-m radius, the paired difference over 2,780 conforming lots was −0.5 percentage points (95% interval −2.5 to 1.5), so no significant difference was detected, which does not establish equivalence. The additional contribution of the geometry-aware covariance was isolated by a paired ablation with identical measurements, three new checks per lot, and separately calibrated thresholds, in which only the kernel differed: a stationary straight-route kernel against the geometry-aware kernel of Eq. (5). At closely matched consumer risks (differences of at most 0.5 percentage points), the producer risk fell from 44.1% to 40.6% on the 50-m radius (paired difference 3.5 percentage points, 95% interval 2.6–4.5) and from 75.3% to 55.0% on the 15-m radius (20.3, 95% interval 18.4–22.2); on straight routes the two kernels coincide and the risks were identical. Under the tested curved-route scenarios, the ablation thus isolates the additional reduction in producer risk attributable to the geometry-aware covariance, which grows with curvature; it does not by itself explain every difference between the integrated method and other methods.
Selection and evaluation of plans used independent three-lot replicates in which only the central lot is counted, with separate selection lots (4,800 per candidate ) and evaluation lots (4,800), so that the conditions of Proposition 4 hold (Table 3, Fig. 6a). Without a margin, the evaluated consumer risks of the selected plans were 0.082–0.117, and for the floor-layout specification the target was exceeded (0.117, 95% interval 0.095–0.143). With thresholds selected under a DKW margin shared by the four candidate plans, the evaluated consumer risks were 0.019–0.072, all upper confidence limits below 0.10, at the price of producer risks of 0.126–0.286; for the analyzed parameters and the strict-alignment variant no candidate met the producer-risk target of 0.15 with the margin, and the engine flagged them as infeasible. In 12 end-to-end replicates,  and  were identified by maximum likelihood from ten 500-m control-line passes, a plan was synthesized with the lower bound of , and it was applied to 1,960 new interior lots with a random bias. With a correct Gauss–Markov model, the realized consumer risk was 0.028–0.077 (median 0.040); with a smooth second-order truth analyzed with the first-order model, it exceeded the target in 5 of 12 replicates (maximum 0.124). The covariance family, not only its parameters, must be identified.
In all alignment results, as in the discrimination study, the first and last lot of each run are excluded, because with a single kriging neighbor they would need their own calibration. The margin was selected on the 490 interior lots of a development run (five closed-loop runs of 10 km, seed 2027) by a stated rule, the smallest margin that leaves at most one of the 12 development violations unflagged, which gave  mm (Table S16). All margins were evaluated on the 4,900 interior lots of 50 further independent runs with separate seeds (38 and 380), not used for the selection. Of these, 119 lots violated the alignment target and 91 passed the position test (Table S22, Fig. 6b). Without a margin, the screen left 75 of the 91 in outcome A. With  mm, all 91 were flagged, and the complete procedure accepted 3 of 91 (3.3%). The binomial reference interval assuming independent lots is 0.7–9.3%. The lots are, however, clustered in 41 runs; as sensitivity analyses, a design-effect adjustment (design effect 1.00, estimated from only three events) leaves it unchanged, and a percentile bootstrap over whole runs (2,000 replicates of the pooled ratio) gives 0.0–8.1%. Three misses observed in 91 relevant lots do not provide a sufficient basis to claim a miss rate below 10% with 95% confidence.
What a field campaign must supply is site-specific input, and the method places field data where they are most informative. The covariance family, the failure mode of Table S20, was selected correctly by likelihood from control-line passes in all 60 replicates for each family, already with five passes of 500 m (lower 95% bound 0.94; Table S18), and ten passes bound  within 73–132 m. Demonstrating the consumer risk directly on field lots is, by contrast, impractical: showing a risk below 0.10 with 95% confidence and 80% power when the true risk is 0.05 needs about 180 independent nonconforming lots, roughly 700 lots at the nonconforming share of the simulations. As in acceptance sampling by variables, the risk is therefore calibrated on the identified model, and the field check is a predictive check of that model: about 125 held-out survey points detect a drop of the 95% prediction-interval coverage to 90%.

reduction in producer risk attributable to the geometry-aware covariance, which grows with

Selection and evaluation of plans used independent three-lot replicates in which only the
central lot is counted, with separate selection lots (4,800 per candidate 𝑘) and evaluation lots
(4,800), so that the conditions of Proposition 4 hold (Table 3, Fig. 6a). Without a margin, the
evaluated consumer risks of the selected plans were 0.082–0.117, and for the floor-layout
specification the target was exceeded (0.117, 95% interval 0.095–0.143). With thresholds
selected under a DKW margin shared by the four candidate plans, the evaluated consumer risks
were 0.019–0.072, all upper confidence limits below 0.10, at the price of producer risks of
0.126–0.286; for the analyzed parameters and the strict-alignment variant no candidate met the
producer-risk target of 0.15 with the margin, and the engine flagged them as infeasible. In 12
end-to-end replicates, 𝜎" and ℓ" were identified by maximum likelihood from ten 500-m controlline passes, a plan was synthesized with the lower bound of ℓ" , and it was applied to 1,960 new
interior lots with a random bias. With a correct Gauss–Markov model, the realized consumer risk
was 0.028–0.077 (median 0.040); with a smooth second-order truth analyzed with the first-order
model, it exceeded the target in 5 of 12 replicates (maximum 0.124). The covariance family, not
only its parameters, must be identified.
In all alignment results, as in the discrimination study, the first and last lot of each run are
excluded, because with a single kriging neighbor they would need their own calibration. The
margin was selected on the 490 interior lots of a development run (five closed-loop runs of 10
km, seed 2027) by a stated rule, the smallest margin that leaves at most one of the 12
development violations unflagged, which gave 𝑚 = 6 mm (Table S16). All margins were
evaluated on the 4,900 interior lots of 50 further independent runs with separate seeds (38 and

 380), not used for the selection. Of these, 119 lots violated the alignment target and 91 passed the
position test (Table S22, Fig. 6b). Without a margin, the screen left 75 of the 91 in outcome A.
With 𝑚 = 6 mm, all 91 were flagged, and the complete procedure accepted 3 of 91 (3.3%). The
binomial reference interval assuming independent lots is 0.7–9.3%. The lots are, however,
clustered in 41 runs; as sensitivity analyses, a design-effect adjustment (design effect 1.00,
estimated from only three events) leaves it unchanged, and a percentile bootstrap over whole
runs (2,000 replicates of the pooled ratio) gives 0.0–8.1%. Three misses observed in 91 relevant
lots do not provide a sufficient basis to claim a miss rate below 10% with 95% confidence.
What a field campaign must supply is site-specific input, and the method places field data
where they are most informative. The covariance family, the failure mode of Table S20, was
selected correctly by likelihood from control-line passes in all 60 replicates for each family,
already with five passes of 500 m (lower 95% bound 0.94; Table S18), and ten passes bound ℓ"
within 73–132 m. Demonstrating the consumer risk directly on field lots is, by contrast,
impractical: showing a risk below 0.10 with 95% confidence and 80% power when the true risk
is 0.05 needs about 180 independent nonconforming lots, roughly 700 lots at the nonconforming
share of the simulations. As in acceptance sampling by variables, the risk is therefore calibrated
on the identified model, and the field check is a predictive check of that model: about 125 heldout survey points detect a drop of the 95% prediction-interval coverage to 90%.
